success_patterns: Verbatim archive or lyric hit: the clue text appears word-for-word in several passages (J-Archive style 'DALLAS | clue | Bobby Ewing', lyric pages), and the agent copied the answer exactly as the passages give it.

Slot-type discipline: 'this woman's gallery' gave a person (Peggy Guggenheim), 'this newspaper' gave a newspaper title, 'this novel' gave a title, and a list of character names gave the series. Each answer was the owner or container entity, never an anchor from the clue.
Leading articles that belong to a proper title were kept ('The New York Times', 'The Outsiders'). Full person names were used when the passages repeat them.
Clue that lists its own options: the agent returned one option verbatim ('South Park').

Quoted-lyric clue: the agent completed the quote with the exact multi-word continuation that recurs across passages ('rosy red'). It did not shorten it to one colour word, even though Rule 4 usually favours dropping modifiers.

patch.reasoning: Nearly every success pattern is already covered by Rules 1-4 and the strategic guidance, so a large patch would only add length and risk. The one gap is a latent conflict: Rule 4 says to drop modifiers and give the shortest form, but for a quoted lyric or line the answer is the literal continuation, whose multi-word form should be kept (rosy red, not red). One short bullet resolves that conflict without touching any rule that drives the stable passes.

edits.target: - If the clue is a fragment, work out what single thing connects it to the context.
edits.content: - Quoted lyric / quotation clues ('"The object of my affection can change my complexion from white" to this color'): the answer is the literal continuation of the quote. Find the line repeated across the passages and copy the words that follow the quoted fragment exactly, even if they are two words ('rosy red', not 'red'). The 'drop modifiers' rules in Rule 4 do not apply to quoted continuations.
